newsitem.title: THAILAND: FEATURE - Thailand haven for designer label fakes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Thailand haven for designer label fakes.

text.p: The plainclothes police pushed open the door of the back alley building, crossed the urine soaked room and bounded up the stairs.
The workers on the second floor looked up but did not pause at their sewing machines as the police searched the room and the radio blared.
After a quick look, some of the officers continued up to the third floor.
"Nothing," said one looking in on a nearly empty room. He returned downstairs to find one of his colleagues pulling piles of dress shirts carrying the Polo brand name from under a table.

"Ah, the old under-the-table trick," said Russell Lerner, general manager of Pinkerton Consulting and Investigation Services, as he looked through a bag of fake Polo labels the machinist had been sewing on to the shirts.
The raid, a small one by Pinkerton standards, was one of several hundred carried out each year in Thailand as companies try to stem the multi-billion dollar counterfeit business.
The raids are on all sorts of suppliers, from small shops to large factories. Many are situated in back alleys and employ underage workers or illegal aliens.

"American and European designers, software houses and manufacturers of all kind are having products knocked off in Thailand and other countries in Asia," Lerner said, sitting next to a huge pile of fake jeans confiscated in a previous raid.
U.S.-based Pinkerton has an office in Bangkok and investigates claims of copyright and intellectual property violations on behalf of clients from all over the world.
Once it has gathered enough information, Pinkerton works with local police to organise raids on factories and retail outlets to confiscate fake goods and stop production.

"Many of our clients say Thailand is one of the number one areas of concern in Asia. It's at that stage of development," Lerner said. "Most countries go through a stage where they're growing quite quickly economically but somehow lack the local expertise and creativity to come up with their own designs."
American jean maker Levi Strauss & Co is one of the companies actively working to stamp out fake products in Asia.

"We are very concerned with Thailand because Thailand is a recognised country where counterfeits are being made for local use and export," Wai Zee, Singapore-based intellectual property attorney for Levi Strauss, told Reuters.
All types of fake Levi jeans, complete with the small red trademark label on the back pocket, can be bought in Bangkok's street markets for a fraction of the cost of the real thing.
One of Pinkerton's clients estimates about half of the local market for jeans is held by counterfeits of all brands.
"Of about 15 million pairs of jeans sold in Thailand a year, approximately half of those sold are counterfeit," Lerner said.
"What you see on the street is just the tip of the iceberg. There are containers of counterfeit products of all types going out of Thailand every day."
Knock-off products ranging from garments to computer software, cosmetics, video and audio tapes make their way from Thailand to eastern Europe or Africa, Lerner said.
A Thai official said the government has taken steps to enforce copyright laws and suppress production of counterfeit goods.
"We are cooperating with copyright holders to capture and seize these goods," Pajchima Thanasanti, director of the coordinating center for Supression of Intellectual Property Violation, told Reuters.
But others say that although Thailand has made great strides over the past few years by passing copyright and patent laws, enforcement is still a problem.

The United States, which has Thailand on a watch list to monitor progress and implementation of intellectual property right commitments, plans an "out of cycle review" on Thailand in October because it is concerned.

"We believe that Thailand has made substantial strides in protection of intellectual property," a U.S. Embassy spokesperson said. "However, despite the progress...concerns remain, including a drop in enforcement in 1995, and the need to ensure deterrent penalties are imposed on convicted pirates."
One problem in Thailand, and in other Asian nations, is that counterfeiting is not viewed as a major crime, Lerner said.

"It doesn't have the same stigma attached to it that would prevent people from dealing in drugs or prostitution," he said. "It's a soft crime. They mostly view themselves as businessmen, out to make a buck. It's a victimless crime in their minds. No one gets hurt, no one gets killed.
"Police, courts, prosecuters -- their sympathies still lie pretty much with the small guy, the guy that's trying to do business." he said.
